topic.subject: science
topic.title: Components of food
topic.scope: carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, roughage, water, balanced diet, deficiency diseases, food tests

nodes.name: Fats provide more energy than carbs

misconceptions.statement: Vitamins provide energy to the body for playing and running.
misconceptions.why: Students often associate anything 'healthy' or 'protective' with the immediate feeling of energy.
misconceptions.fix: Vitamins do not provide energy; they help protect our body against diseases and keep our eyes, bones, and gums healthy. Carbohydrates and fats are the actual energy providers.

probe.question: If you feel tired and need immediate energy, should you eat a vitamin pill or a bowl of rice?

misconceptions.root_belief: all beneficial things perform the same function

misconceptions.statement: Fats are always harmful and should be completely removed from our diet.
misconceptions.why: Everyday health warnings about obesity lead students to view fats as purely toxic substances.
misconceptions.fix: Fats are essential nutrients that provide more energy than carbohydrates. We need them in small quantities for a healthy body.

probe.question: Is a diet with zero grams of fat the healthiest diet for a growing child?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because fat only makes people fat.

misconceptions.root_belief: substances are either purely good or purely bad

misconceptions.statement: Roughage is a nutrient that helps us grow taller.
misconceptions.why: Students assume all components of food must be 'nutrients' that contribute to growth.
misconceptions.fix: Roughage (dietary fibre) is not a nutrient and does not provide growth; it is the undigested part of food that helps our body get rid of waste.

probe.question: What is the main job of roughage in our food?
probe.wrong_answer: To help us grow and build muscles.

misconceptions.statement: A balanced diet means eating equal amounts of every nutrient.
misconceptions.why: The word 'balanced' is interpreted as 'mathematically equal' rather than 'proportionally appropriate'.
misconceptions.fix: A balanced diet contains different nutrients in the specific proportions our body needs, not in equal amounts. For example, we need more carbohydrates than vitamins.

probe.question: If you eat 100g of fats, 100g of vitamins, and 100g of proteins, is that a balanced diet?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because all amounts are equal and balanced.

misconceptions.source_hint: HBCSE research on student ideas about diet

misconceptions.statement: Deficiency diseases like scurvy can spread from one person to another by coughing.
misconceptions.why: Students overgeneralize the concept of 'disease' to mean 'germ-based infection'.
misconceptions.fix: Deficiency diseases are caused by a lack of nutrients and are not communicable. You cannot 'catch' them from someone else.

probe.question: If your friend has night blindness, can you get it by sitting next to them?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because it is a disease.

misconceptions.root_belief: all diseases are caused by germs
misconceptions.source_hint: Rosalind Driver's Children's Ideas in Science

misconceptions.statement: Washing vegetables after cutting them makes them cleaner and healthier.
misconceptions.why: Students focus on the visible removal of dirt without understanding the invisible loss of vitamins.
misconceptions.fix: Washing vegetables after cutting them leads to the loss of many water-soluble vitamins. It is better to wash them before cutting.

probe.question: Why should we avoid washing peeled and chopped vegetables?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the water will make the vegetables dirty again.

misconceptions.root_belief: more cleaning always leads to better health

misconceptions.statement: The iron in our food is the same as the hard metal used to make nails.
misconceptions.why: Literal interpretation of the word 'iron' based on everyday objects.
misconceptions.fix: The iron in food is a mineral in a chemical form that our body can absorb to make blood; it is not tiny pieces of hard metal.

probe.question: If a food is rich in iron, does it mean it contains small metal pieces?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, that is why it makes our body strong like metal.

misconceptions.root_belief: a word means its everyday meaning

misconceptions.statement: The iodine test turns food blue-black if it contains any kind of sugar.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the specific carbohydrate 'starch' with the general category of 'sugar'.
misconceptions.fix: The iodine test specifically detects starch. It does not turn blue-black for simple sugars like glucose.

probe.question: Will a solution of plain table sugar turn blue-black when iodine is added?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, because sugar is a carbohydrate.

misconceptions.root_belief: a test for a part works for the whole

misconceptions.statement: We only get water for our body when we drink it from a glass.
misconceptions.why: Students only account for visible, direct consumption of liquids.
misconceptions.fix: Our body gets water not just from drinking, but also from many food items like fruits, vegetables, and even milk or tea.

probe.question: If you eat a juicy watermelon, are you providing water to your body?
probe.wrong_answer: No, you are only eating food, not drinking.

misconceptions.root_belief: what you cannot see does not exist

misconceptions.statement: If a food item does not leave an oily mark on paper, it contains no fats.
misconceptions.why: Reliance on the simplest physical test without considering hidden or bound fats.
misconceptions.fix: While the paper test is a good indicator, some foods have very small amounts of fat or 'hidden' fats that might not leave a visible oily patch easily.

probe.question: Can a food have fat even if it doesn't feel greasy to touch?
probe.wrong_answer: No, fat must always be oily and visible.

misconceptions.root_belief: physical properties are always immediately apparent

misconceptions.statement: Only people who want to build big muscles need to eat protein.
misconceptions.why: Association of protein with gym culture and bodybuilding supplements.
misconceptions.fix: Everyone needs protein for the basic repair of damaged body tissues and for general growth, not just for building large muscles.

probe.question: Does a child who doesn't exercise still need protein?
probe.wrong_answer: No, because they are not trying to be a bodybuilder.

misconceptions.root_belief: specialized use cases apply to everyone

misconceptions.statement: Eating a huge amount of Vitamin A can cure a broken bone.
misconceptions.why: General belief that 'vitamins' are a magic cure-all for any physical injury.
misconceptions.fix: Specific nutrients prevent specific deficiencies. Vitamin A is for vision; Calcium and Vitamin D are needed for bones.

probe.question: Which nutrient would specifically help strengthen weak bones?
